questions.question: In this cohort study, when was the excess hazard of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in cancer patients greatest?
options: Uniformly across the entire follow-up period
Within the first year after cancer diagnosis
Only once metastatic disease developed
Between 1 and 5 years after diagnosis
questions.explanation: The hazard was strongest in the first year after diagnosis, with lung and neurological cancers showing roughly 6-fold short-term excess, though risk stayed elevated over longer follow-up. As a register-based study, it can't explain why arrests occurred, so treat this as context rather than a change to practice.

questions.question: In this registry study of OHCA patients whose initial non-shockable rhythm converted to shockable, what did amiodarone show for neurological outcome at discharge?
options: Improved neurological outcome only in patients who survived to 24 hours
No statistically significant difference, though the trend favoured amiodarone
A statistically significant worsening of neurological outcome
A statistically significant improvement in favourable neurological outcome
questions.explanation: Favourable neurological outcome was 3.7% vs 2.9%, which didn't reach statistical significance. This is retrospective registry data with residual confounding, so the survival benefit remains an association rather than proof.

questions.question: Among visits with a recorded discharge diagnosis, which diagnosis group carried a higher risk of death during follow-up than confirmed STEMI?
options: NSTE-ACS or other coronary syndromes
Other cardiac diagnoses
Noncardiac diagnoses
Symptom-based diagnoses
questions.explanation: Noncardiac diagnoses had higher adjusted mortality during follow-up (HR 1.75) than confirmed STEMI, while the other groups did not differ materially. The data are retrospective registry coded diagnoses, so treat these comparisons as descriptive context.

questions.short_title: Ice-water immersion wins for drug hyperthermia
questions.question: For a hyperthermic patient with suspected amfetamine toxicity, which cooling method did the review identify as most practical when immersion isn't feasible?
options: Passive cooling in shade with fanning
Room temperature water immersion at 0.089 ± 0.020 °C/min
Ice packs applied to the groin and axillae
Ice water-soaked sheets or towels, which cooled at 0.121 ± 0.030 °C/min
questions.explanation: Ice water-soaked sheets or towels were the fastest non-immersion option and are feasible in most pre-hospital and ED settings while allowing monitoring. The evidence is limited because many included studies involved exercise-induced rather than drug-induced hyperthermia.

questions.short_title: Little evidence for call handler wellbeing programs
questions.question: What did this systematic review conclude about interventions aimed at supporting emergency call handlers' wellbeing and job satisfaction?
options: Moderate evidence for residential recovery programs only
Limited evidence of effectiveness, with no role-specific programs validated
Clear evidence that multicomponent programs reduce stress
Strong evidence that resilience training improves wellbeing
questions.explanation: Across 12 studies in four intervention categories, there was limited evidence any intervention improved health, wellbeing or stress outcomes. Most studies measured mental health only, mixed call handlers with first responders, and varied in quality, so no call handler-specific program has been validated.

questions.short_title: Paediatric OHCA in Australia and NZ: Aus-ROC report
questions.question: In this Australasian registry of paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, what proportion of EMS-attended cases received bystander CPR, and how did bystander defibrillation compare?
options: About 63% received bystander CPR but only 1.6% got bystander defibrillation
About 40% received bystander CPR and 1.6% got bystander defibrillation
About 63% received bystander CPR and about half got bystander defibrillation
About 75% received bystander CPR and about 60% got bystander defibrillation
questions.explanation: Bystander CPR was provided in 62.7% of EMS-attended cases, yet bystander defibrillation was rare at 1.6%. Cases were mostly unwitnessed and occurred in private residences, which helps explain the low defibrillation rate.

questions.short_title: Redirecting non-urgent patients to primary care looks safe
questions.question: In the scoping review of redirecting non-urgent ED patients to primary care, what distinguished the studies that reported zero hospitalisations and deaths?
options: They only redirected patients under 40 with normal vital signs
They all followed patients for at least 30 days after redirection
They were the only studies that randomised patients to redirection
They used a richer set of implementation components around triage and documentation
questions.explanation: The studies with no hospitalisations or deaths included the fullest range of implementation components, such as triage, vital signs and documentation. Overall safety numbers were reassuring, but the evidence was mostly observational with heterogeneous models and short follow-up.

questions.question: In this pooled analysis of prehospital TXA trials, which patient group appeared to benefit most from TXA?
options: Patients with hyperfibrinolysis (LY30 above 3%)
Patients with traumatic brain injury regardless of fibrinolysis status
Patients with physiological fibrinolysis (LY30 0.9–3%)
Patients with fibrinolytic shutdown (LY30 below 0.9%)
questions.explanation: Shutdown patients given TXA had roughly a third the risk of death (HR 0.32). Treat this as hypothesis-generating only: the fibrinolysis phenotypes were measured on hospital arrival, not prehospital, and this was a subgroup analysis of pooled trials.
